title: Bifurcation of laser-dressed band extrema in solids under intense low-frequency fields
authors: Alexander Flegel, Liang-Wen Pi, Liang-You Peng, Mikhail Frolov
abstract: We show that an intense low-frequency laser field can qualitatively modify the local extremal structure of an interband energy gap in a crystal. Using an instantaneous laser-dressed basis obtained from the nonperturbative diagonalization of the multiband crystal Hamiltonian, we derive a quartic normal form for the dressed gap near a high-symmetry point. At a critical field, the quadratic part of this normal form changes sign, and the gap experiences a bifurcation: a single symmetric minimum splits into two symmetry-related minima separated by a local maximum. We identify the microscopic origin of this bifurcation by decomposing the quadratic part into a homogeneous Stark contribution and a field-modified band-curvature contribution. The latter originates from the multiband redistribution of interband polarizations and provides the mechanism for the field-induced change of the gap extrema. A realization for the Kronig--Penney model demonstrates the same bifurcation at multiple high-symmetry points and for different interband gaps. As an illustration of its spectral consequences, we show that the bifurcation gives rise to an additional van Hove feature in the instantaneous interband susceptibility above the absorption edge. Our results establish a general mechanism by which strong-field dressing modifies the local geometry of the electronic spectrum.
summary: This paper theoretically demonstrates that intense, low-frequency laser fields can induce a qualitative bifurcation in the energy gap structure of crystalline solids. This phenomenon, which changes the local minimum geometry, is driven by field-modified band curvature and is spectroscopically observable as an additional feature in the interband susceptibility.
main_problem: The study investigates how an intense, low-frequency laser field can qualitatively alter the local extremal structure of the interband energy gap within a crystalline solid.
main_result: The gap exhibits a bifurcation at a critical field strength, where a single minimum splits into two symmetry-related minima separated by a local maximum. This is signaled spectroscopically by the emergence of an additional van Hove feature in the interband susceptibility.
method: The authors derive a quartic normal form for the dressed gap near a high-symmetry point and analyze the system using an instantaneous laser-dressed basis obtained from nonperturbative diagonalization of the multiband Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to the electronic structure of solids, using the 1D Kronig-Penney model as a concrete realization. The dynamics are governed by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation under the influence of a strong, low-frequency laser field.
key_observables: Local extremal structure of the interband gap, interband susceptibility ($	ilde{\chi}$), and the bifurcation point ($F^{(cr)}$).
important_parameters: Intense low-frequency laser field strength ($F_t$), crystal momentum ($K_t$), and the critical field strength ($F^{(cr)}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on an adiabatic approximation, assuming the field-dressed Hamiltonian varies slowly compared to interband energy scales, and focuses on the instantaneous spectral structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the bifurcation structure of the dressed gap $	ilde{\Delta}_{10}(K_t, F_t)$ and show the spectral evolution of the interband susceptibility $	ilde{\chi}(\Omega; F_	au)$ across the critical field.
paper_structure: The paper develops the formalism by establishing the instantaneous laser-dressed basis, deriving the normal form for the gap, identifying the microscopic origin of the bifurcation (field-modified band-curvature contribution), and finally demonstrating the spectral consequences using the Kronig-Penney model.
why_interesting: This work provides a general, non-perturbative mechanism for how strong-field dressing modifies the local geometry of the electronic spectrum, which is highly relevant for understanding ultrafast spectroscopy and light-matter interactions in solids.
